metric_rationale: By isolating trials where Tallying encounters a tie (i.e., both options win on an equal number of features), we can cleanly separate the two theories. Tallying predicts random guessing (0.5) on these trials regardless of its parameters. In contrast, WADD uses the specific validities to break the tie, consistently favoring the option with higher validity-weighted features. Measuring the proportion of choices that align with WADD's prediction on these specific tie trials yields exactly 0.5 for Tallying and strictly > 0.5 for WADD.

The metric contrasts the probability of choosing option B on two specific trial types where Tallying and WADD systematically diverge. On both Trial 4 and Trial 9, each option has exactly one unique winning feature, so Tallying always registers a tie and predicts a 50/50 choice (difference = 0). However, WADD weighs features by their validities. In Trial 4, B's unique advantage (0.78) outweighs A's (0.55), leading WADD to favor B. In Trial 9, A's unique advantage (0.95) heavily outweighs B's (0.55), leading WADD to favor A. Thus, WADD predicts a positive difference (P(B|Trial 4) - P(B|Trial 9) > 0), whereas Tallying predicts exactly zero.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that exactly align with the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic's predictions. TTB strictly follows the validity order of features (0, 2, 1, 3). WADD, on the other hand, allows for subjective weighting of validities (via the `weights` parameter) and compensatory evaluation, meaning it will frequently deviate from the rigid lexicographic choice pattern of TTB. Thus, data simulated under TTB will have a much higher TTB-match proportion than data simulated under WADD.

Trial 11 is specifically designed to pit a single higher-validity cue against multiple lower-validity cues. TTB will predictably choose the option with the single higher-validity cue (feature 1, validity 0.84), while WADD's compensatory nature allows the combined weight of the two lower-validity cues (validities 0.64 and 0.55) to outvote it. By computing the proportion of choices that align with the TTB prediction on this specific trial, we obtain a metric that is high for TTB and low for WADD, cleanly discriminating the two theories.

This metric calculates the difference in the rate at which subjects choose the option favored by the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic between two types of trials: 'unanimous' trials (where all discriminating cues point to the same option) and 'conflict' trials (where some lesser cues point to the opposite option). For the TTB model, the presence of conflicting lesser cues is entirely ignored, meaning the probability of choosing the TTB option is identical across both trial types (yielding an expected difference of 0, governed only by the constant lapse rate epsilon). For the Probabilistic TTB (PTTB) model, conflicting cues attract choice probability proportional to their validities, meaning the model will choose the TTB option less frequently in conflict trials than in unanimous trials (yielding an expected difference strictly greater than 0).

This metric calculates the proportion of times a subject's choice aligns with the highest validity cue (Cue 0, validity 0.95) specifically on trials where it is opposed by the second highest validity cue (Cue 2, validity 0.88). TTB strictly follows the highest validity cue, so it will almost always choose the option favored by Cue 0 on these trials. PTTB, however, samples cues probabilistically based on their validities. Because 0.95 and 0.88 are very close, PTTB has a substantial probability of sampling Cue 2 first and thus choosing the option favored by Cue 2, leading to a visibly lower alignment with Cue 0.

In this specific experimental setup, the log-odds weights for the features are strictly non-compensatory. Thus, the Naive Bayes / WADD model and the Take-The-Best (TTB) model will make the exact same deterministic 'core' choice on every trial. The difference lies in how they scale choice probabilities. TTB relies solely on a constant lapse rate, meaning the probability of choosing the TTB-favored option is independent of the margin of evidence. In contrast, WADD uses a softmax rule where the probability of choosing the favored option depends on the difference in log-odds values. By comparing the proportion of TTB-consistent choices on trials with a very large log-odds margin against trials with a very small log-odds margin, we can cleanly separate the theories: TTB predicts a difference of 0, while WADD predicts a positive difference.

Both WADD (with log-odds validities) and TTB predict the exact same choice on all 16 unique trials, because the log-odds weights for these specific validities form a strictly lexicographic sequence. However, they differ in their predicted choice probabilities. TTB predicts a constant accuracy across all trials (determined only by the lapse rate epsilon). WADD predicts that choice accuracy scales with the difference in the options' subjective values. By contrasting the empirical accuracy on trials with a large WADD score difference versus trials with a small WADD score difference, we can perfectly distinguish the two theories: TTB predicts a difference of 0, whereas WADD predicts a strictly positive difference.
